title: We Three Kings of Orient Are
description: John Henry Hopkins Jr.'s carol of the three kings, words and tune his own, from his Carols, Hymns, and Songs (New York, [1863?]), for 2 to 4 singers: verses 1 and 5, the two his book gives to all three kings together, each followed by the Chorus, "O Star of Wonder". The verse walks in E minor and the Chorus turns to G major, with the lower parts adapted from Hopkins's own trio and chorus.

credits.arrangement: John Henry Hopkins Jr.'s trio and chorus (1863), adapted by Stackapella

licence.arrangement: John Henry Hopkins Jr.'s own harmony (public domain: Hopkins died 1891), adapted for 2 to 4 beginners: the verse from his trio and its accompaniment, the Chorus from his four parts. Kept: his tune (Gaspard's part and the Chorus's top line) in his key and every note of it, his chords, his alto in the verse (Melchior's part) and the bass of his accompaniment. Changed: the alto rises D-sharp, E, F-sharp, G under "O-ri-ent are" and "tra-verse a-far" and E, F-sharp, G under "yon-der Star" (Melchior's D-sharp, D-sharp, D-sharp, E and E, D-sharp, E), so it ends each line a third above the tune's low E, and sings one note a syllable, B4 then G4, under "moun-tain" (his B, A, G); the tenor is ours, below the alto (Balthazar's D, C and B under "fountain", "Following" and "yonder"); the bass holds G2 under "Moor and moun-tain", where the accompaniment walks B3, A3, G3; in the Chorus the alto takes B3 under the tune's G4 wherever his alto has D4 ("Star of Won-", "Night", "Star with Roy-", "bright", "Guide us to", "Light"), so the duet has the third, with D4 on "der", "al" and "Thy" (his B3), C4 on "O" (his D4), E4 on "Still" and D4 on "pro-" and the last "ing" (his G4); the tenor sits under it (G3 for his B3, F-sharp 3 for his C4 on "O", C4 for his E4 on "Still", G3, A3, G3 under "pro-ceed-ing", E3 on "per-", E3 on the last "fect" and D3 on the last "Light"); the bass sings G2 for his G3 in "Star of Won-", "Star with Roy-" and "Guide us to", B2 under "der", "al", "Thy" and the last "ing", and D3 under "pro-"; the piano interlude after the Chorus is left out; breaths written in for beginners (the verse's last "Star" a quarter beat shorter, "ceed-ing" sung as a dotted figure with a breath before "Guide", and the first Chorus's "Light" two beats then a breath); the tenor holds B3 under "O-ri-ent are", "tra-verse a-far", "be-hold Him a-rise" and "Sa-cri-fice", so each line-end E minor chord has its fifth; accepted exception: the duet keeps his alto's E under the tune's A on "Fol-low-ing" and "lu-jah the" (a bare fourth; the C is in the bass at 3 singers and the tenor at 4); the soprano and tenor octaves G to B at the start of verse 5 (beat 96) come across the breath after the first Chorus's "Light", and are not heard as consecutive.
licence.source: John H. Hopkins, Jr., Carols, Hymns, and Songs (New York: Church Book Depository, 762 Broadway; the title page undated, catalogued [1863?], the earliest printing we have seen), "Three Kings of Orient", pp. 12 and 13: the verse for three voices headed Gaspard, Melchior and Balthazar (in the G clef, "for the accommodation of children", men's voices preferred) over a piano accompaniment, then a four-part Chorus and an Interlude, in E minor turning to G major, in 3/8; written here in E minor in 3/4, each quaver a crotchet beat; verses 1 and 5 as printed under the music (the book's note: verses 1 and 5 are sung as a trio, verses 2, 3 and 4 as solos to Gaspard's part), "Sa-" over two quavers as the page places it, the small capitals of "King", "God" and "Sacrifice" set in ordinary type; Princeton Theological Seminary Library copy (Louis F. Benson's), read from the scan at archive.org/details/carolshym00hopk/page/n19 and n20; the same music compared in the 1872 printing (pp. 12 and 13, archive.org/details/hyolsongs00hopk/page/n19) and the 1882 one (pp. 18 and 19, archive.org/details/carolsh00hopk/page/n23 and n24, which dates the carol "1857"); both print "Al-le-lu-ia" where the 1863 page sings "Hal-le-lu-jah", which we keep
